notes.2.6.524: 6.552: 'he will commit what he himself could inform on' is uncertain; the sense may be that he commits crimes he could denounce in others. 6.589: literally 'who shows long gold on bare neck'; the point of the line is unclear. 6.614a–c are numbered as additional lines; they interrupt the construction 'if you do not ... begin to rave' (614, 615), and 614c in particular is obscure, so the passage looks interpolated or disturbed.

nodes.text: eddies she will rinse her timid head; then over the whole field
of the proud king, naked and trembling, on bloody
knees she will crawl; if white Io commands it,
she will go to the ends of Egypt, and water fetched from hot
Meroe she will carry back, to sprinkle in the temple
of Isis that rises right beside the old sheepfold.
For she believes she is warned by the voice of the Lady herself:
there's a soul and mind for gods to chat with at night!
So the foremost and highest honour is earned by the one
who, ringed by his linen-clad flock and his bald flock,
runs along as Anubis, mocking the breast-beating people.
He begs pardon whenever the wife has not abstained
from sex on the holy days that must be kept,
and a great penalty is owed for the defiled bedspread,
and the silver serpent was seen to move its head;
his tears and well-rehearsed mutterings make sure
that pardon for the fault is not refused, bought off by a fat goose,
no doubt, and a thin cake, by Osiris.
When he has made way, leaving behind her basket and hay,
a trembling Jewess begs, whispering in her private ear,
an interpreter of the laws of Jerusalem and high priestess
of the tree, and faithful go-between of highest heaven.
She too gets her palm filled, but more meagrely; for a tiny coin
the Jews will sell you any dreams you like.
A tender lover is promised, or a childless rich man's
huge will, once the lung of a warm dove
has been handled, by an Armenian or Commagenian entrail-reader;
he will probe the breasts of chickens, the guts of a puppy,
sometimes even of a boy; he will commit what he himself could inform on.
But the Chaldaeans will be trusted more: whatever
an astrologer says, they will believe was brought from the spring
of Ammon, since at Delphi the oracles have fallen silent
and darkness about the future condemns the human race.
Yet the chief of them is the one who has often been exiled,
through whose friendship and chart for hire
a great citizen died, one whom Otho feared.
That is what gives his art credit: if his right hand has clanked with iron
and his left, if he has lain long in a military prison;
no astrologer will be thought to have a genius unless he has been condemned,
but only one who nearly died, who barely managed to be sent to the Cyclades
and at last got free of little Seriphos.
She consults about the lingering death of her jaundiced mother,
but about you first, your Tanaquil does: when she will bury her sister
and her uncles, and whether her lover is going to live
after her: for what greater gift can the gods give?
This one, though, does not know what the gloomy star
of Saturn threatens, in what constellation happy Venus shows herself,
which month is given to losses, which times to gain:
remember also to avoid running into the woman
in whose hands you see, worn smooth like sticky amber,
her almanacs; who consults no one, but is now
consulted herself; who, when her husband sets out for camp or home,
will not go with him, called back by the numbers of Thrasyllus.
When she fancies a ride out to the first milestone, the hour
is taken from the book; if the rubbed corner of her eye
itches, she inspects her horoscope and then calls for eye-salve;
though she lies sick, no hour seems fitter
for taking food than the one Petosiris has given.
If she is of middling rank, she will walk the space on both sides
of the turning-posts, and draw lots, and present her forehead and hand
to the seer who calls for a lot of lip-smacking.
Rich women will get their answers from a Phrygian augur, and from an Indian
hired for it; from an expert in the stars and the heavens,
and from some old man who buries the public lightning;
the fate of the common people is laid out in the Circus and on the rampart;
the woman who shows a long gold [chain] on her bare neck
asks, in front of the towers and the dolphin columns,
whether she should drop the tavern-keeper and marry the cloak-seller.
These women, though, at least undergo the danger of childbirth, and all
the labours of nursing they endure, as their fortune presses them;
but hardly any woman lies in childbed on a gilded couch,
so powerful are the arts, so powerful the drugs, of the woman
who makes them barren and, for killing human beings in the womb,
takes the contract. Rejoice, poor wretch, and with your own hand
pass her whatever the drink may be; for if she chose to swell
and trouble her womb with kicking boys, you would
perhaps be the father of an Ethiopian; soon a dark-skinned heir
would fill your will, one you would never want to see in the morning.
I pass over the substituted children, and the joys and prayers often
cheated at the filthy pools, and the pontiffs fetched from there,
and the Salii who will carry the name of the Scauri on a false
body. Shameless Fortune stands by at night,
smiling at the naked infants; she warms them and wraps them in all
the folds of her gown, then hands them over to great houses
and prepares a secret farce for her own amusement; these she loves, on these she
lavishes herself, and always brings them forward as her own nurslings.
One man brings magic chants, another sells Thessalian
love potions, with which she can unhinge her husband's mind
and beat his backside with a slipper. That is why you are losing your wits,
that is the source of your mental fog and your great forgetfulness of things
you did just now. Still, this is bearable, if you do not
always carry water to leaking jars, always
take up that burden with the very urns dripping,
by which, raving, you made a Phalaris out of our king,
and also begin to rave like that uncle of Nero's,
into whom Caesonia poured the whole forehead of a trembling
foal. What woman will not do what an emperor's wife did?
Everything was ablaze and, its frame broken, was collapsing,
no differently than if Juno had made her husband
insane. Less harmful, then, will be Agrippina's
mushroom, since it stopped the heart of only one
old man and sent his trembling head down
into heaven, and his lips running with long drool;
this potion calls for sword and fire, this potion tortures,
this one mangles senators mixed with the blood of knights.
That is what a mare's foal costs, what one poisoner costs.
They hate the children of a concubine: let no one object,
let no one forbid it; now, now it is lawful to kill a stepson.
obeyed his commands when ordered to kill his wife.
Satire XV
Who does not know, Volusius Bithynicus, what monsters mad
Egypt worships? The crocodile is adored by
this region; that one dreads an ibis glutted with snakes;
the golden image of a sacred long-tailed monkey gleams
where magic strings sound from the half-broken Memnon
and ancient Thebes lies in ruins with its hundred gates.
There they venerate cats, here a river fish, there
whole towns venerate a dog, and no one Diana;
it is sacrilege to violate the leek and onion and break them with a bite;
O holy nations, for whom these grow in their gardens
